Heritage walk in Agra: historical places beyond the Taj Mahal

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

A heritage walk in Agra covers the Mughal capital of the 16th and 17th centuries: the Taj Mahal and Agra Fort (both UNESCO sites since 1983), the riverside gardens and tombs on the Yamuna's left bank, the old city around Jama Masjid, and Akbar's tomb at Sikandra. Fatehpur Sikri, a third UNESCO site, is about 40 km away.

We arrange Agra and Fatehpur Sikri visits on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, led by an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi.

Why Agra matters

Agra was a Lodi town before it was a Mughal one. Sikandar Lodi made it his base in the early 16th century, and Babur, Humayun and then Akbar held court here. Under Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan, Agra was one of the largest cities in the Mughal empire, until Shah Jahan moved the court to Delhi in 1648.

Most visitors see the Taj Mahal and leave. The city is better understood as a river city: the Mughal nobility built walled gardens, pavilions and tombs along both banks of the Yamuna, and the Taj is the grandest of them. A walk that follows the river makes sense of why the Taj sits where it does and faces the way it does.

Layers of Agra's history

Before the Mughals, Agra was a fortified Lodi settlement, and little of that period survives above ground. Babur laid out the first Mughal garden in India on the left bank in the 1520s, now known as Ram Bagh (Aram Bagh).

Akbar rebuilt Agra Fort in red sandstone from 1565 and founded Fatehpur Sikri in the 1570s as a new capital, which he left within about 15 years. Jahangir's reign brought the tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula (1622 to 1628), built by Nur Jahan for her father, with fine stone inlay that anticipates the Taj. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal (begun 1632) for Mumtaz Mahal, added white marble palaces inside the fort, and had the Jama Masjid built in his daughter Jahanara's name in 1648.

Later layers include Jat and Maratha control in the 18th century, British cantonment buildings, and the Roman Catholic cemetery with early European graves. The Mughal architecture guide explains how the style developed across these sites.

Places a heritage walk in Agra covers

  1. Taj Mahal 1632 to about 1648

    Shah Jahan's tomb for Mumtaz Mahal; look at the inlay, the calligraphy that enlarges as it rises, and the mosque and guest hall on either side.

  2. Agra Fort 1565 onward

    Akbar's red sandstone fort with Jahangiri Mahal, and Shah Jahan's marble Khas Mahal, Diwan-i-Khas and Musamman Burj.

  3. Jama Masjid, Agra 1648

    Congregational mosque commissioned in Jahanara's name, facing the fort across the railway line.

  4. Kinari Bazaar Mughal period onward

    Old city market lanes behind the Jama Masjid, with havelis and trade streets.

  5. Itmad-ud-Daula's Tomb 1622 to 1628

    Nur Jahan's tomb for her father, often called the Baby Taj, with early white marble and stone inlay.

  6. Chini ka Rauza about 1635

    Tomb of Afzal Khan Shirazi, notable for glazed tile work in a Persian manner.

  7. Ram Bagh 1520s, later altered

    Associated with Babur's first garden in India, with raised walkways and water channels.

  8. Mehtab Bagh Shah Jahan's reign

    Moonlight garden on the left bank, aligned with the Taj; excavated and replanted from the 1990s.

  9. Akbar's Tomb, Sikandra completed about 1613

    Akbar's tomb, finished by Jahangir, with a gateway of inlaid stone and minarets.

  10. Mariam-uz-Zamani's Tomb 1620s

    Tomb of Akbar's wife near Sikandra, in a building that began as a Lodi structure.

  11. Roman Catholic Cemetery, Agra 17th century onward

    Early European graves including the Hessing tomb, a red sandstone tomb in Mughal style.

  12. Fatehpur Sikri 1571 to 1585

    Akbar's walled capital with the Jama Masjid, Buland Darwaza, Panch Mahal and Diwan-i-Khas. About 40 km by road.

Walking routes in Agra

Fort and old city

About 3 hours

Agra Fort → Jama Masjid, Agra → Kinari Bazaar

The left bank gardens

Half a day, by vehicle between stops

Itmad-ud-Daula's Tomb → Chini ka Rauza → Ram Bagh → Mehtab Bagh

Taj and Sikandra

Half a day, by vehicle to Sikandra

Taj Mahal → Akbar's Tomb, Sikandra → Mariam-uz-Zamani's Tomb

Museums in Agra

  • Taj Museum. Small ASI museum inside the Taj complex with Mughal drawings, documents and objects related to the tomb.
  • Fatehpur Sikri archaeological museum. ASI museum at Fatehpur Sikri with finds from excavations at the site.

Best time for a walk

October to March. Arrive at the Taj at opening for softer light and smaller crowds; the Taj is closed on Fridays.

What you see on an Agra walk

At Agra Fort you read three reigns in one place: Akbar's Jahangiri Mahal in carved red sandstone, then Shah Jahan's Khas Mahal and Musamman Burj in white marble. At Itmad-ud-Daula you see pietra dura inlay at small scale before it was used on the Taj. From Mehtab Bagh, across the river, you see the Taj as it was designed to be seen, from a garden on its own axis.

Students learn to read a char bagh garden plan, to tell red sandstone from marble cladding, and to look at calligraphy and inlay up close. For the broader Indo-Islamic background, see Indo-Islamic architecture.

Agra and Fatehpur Sikri for groups

Groups usually see Agra as part of a study tour. Three capitals: Delhi, Agra and Jaipur puts Agra between the two other Mughal and Rajput capitals, and The Golden Triangle with an archaeologist is a private journey for families and small groups. A day at Fatehpur Sikri can be added through Fatehpur Sikri: Mughal urban vision.

Schools can prepare with a classroom lecture such as Reading a temple for comparison, or a Delhi walk at Humayun's Tomb, the model the Taj grew from. Any other combination can be arranged through a study tour built for your group.

Practical advice for school groups

Agra is about three to four hours from Delhi by road or under two hours by fast train, so a day trip is possible but long. An overnight stay lets you see the Taj at opening and Fatehpur Sikri the next morning. The Taj is closed on Fridays. Security at the Taj restricts what can be carried in, so check the ASI website for current rules on bags, food and group entry before you go.

The sites are spread out, so a coach or cabs are needed between Agra Fort, Itmad-ud-Daula, Mehtab Bagh and Sikandra. Walking works within each site and in the old city around Jama Masjid and Kinari Bazaar.

Questions people ask

Which historical places in Agra should a heritage walk include?

The Taj Mahal and Agra Fort first, then Itmad-ud-Daula's tomb and Mehtab Bagh on the opposite bank, Akbar's tomb at Sikandra and the old city around Jama Masjid. Fatehpur Sikri, about 40 km away, needs a separate half day.

How many UNESCO sites are there in Agra?

Three are in or near Agra: Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal, both inscribed in 1983, and Fatehpur Sikri, inscribed in 1986.

Is an Agra heritage walk suitable for schools?

Yes, but plan it as a day trip from Delhi or an overnight study tour. Use a coach between sites, keep each stop to an hour or so, and check the Taj's security rules on bags and food before the visit.

What museums are there in Agra?

The Taj Museum inside the Taj complex and the ASI museum at Fatehpur Sikri are the main ones. For a wider view of Mughal art, combine Agra with the National Museum in Delhi.

Can we combine Agra with Delhi and Jaipur?

Yes. Talaash Heritage arranges study tours and private journeys that link Delhi, Agra and Jaipur with an archaeologist or historian, for schools, colleges, companies and families.
